topic: Fundamental Constants and Mathematical Structure in Turbulence
target_audience: Advanced Undergraduate Physics or Engineering Students

sections.title: Introduction: The Chaos of the Coffee Cup
lecture_lines: Turbulence is chaotic, non-linear, and multi-scale motion.
Cream swirling in coffee demonstrates this complex behavior.
The Reynolds number dictates transition to turbulent flow.

sections.title: The Kolmogorov Cascade: Energy Transfer
lecture_lines: Large eddies break down into smaller energy-containing ones.
Energy cascades down to the smallest viscous scales.
The energy spectrum follows a minus five-thirds law.
animations: Draw large circles representing eddies that split into smaller ones [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/whirlpool.svg].
Animate energy transferring from large to small scales via vectors.
Graph the energy spectrum decaying with a -5/3 slope.

sections.title: The Kolmogorov Constant (C): A Universal Signature
lecture_lines: Kolmogorov's hypothesis assumes local isotropy in turbulence.
A universal constant governs the energy spectrum's shape.
This constant remains identical across all fluid systems.

sections.title: Mathematical Structure: The Dissipation Scale
lecture_lines: The Kolmogorov length scale marks the dissipation limit.
Viscosity dominates, converting kinetic energy into thermal heat.
This is where the turbulent cascade finally ends.
animations: Animate a line scale narrowing down to a single point [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/thermometer.svg].

Show small eddies vanishing at the dissipation limit point.

sections.title: Summary & Real-World Application
lecture_lines: Constants help predict drag without solving every vortex.
Reynolds number, spectra, and scale define turbulence regimes.
These models improve efficiency in engineering real-world designs.
